Lesson 04 / Text Editor GUI in Rust / ~30 minutes

Where Is the Cursor?

Three stages to a Ln/Col readout — and the counting bug hiding underneath it.

Every code editor you've used shows the cursor position in a corner somewhere. Ln 42, Col 7. It looks like the most trivial feature in the product. It isn't, and the reason it isn't is the reason text editing is hard.

egui knows where the cursor is. It will tell you — as a single number, an offset into the text. Turning that number into a line and a column is your job, and doing it right means being precise about what the number counts.

A position in text is not one number, it's three.
Byte offset, character offset, and screen column are all different — and using the wrong one is how editors corrupt files.

Where you're starting

Lesson 3's 65 lines, saving with Ctrl+S. Check against lesson 3's checkpoint if you're unsure.

adding    removing    existing code, shown only for context

Ask egui what it knows

The editor reports the cursor's raw offset — or says there isn't one.

So far you've drawn the text box with ui.add(…), which hands back only whether it was clicked. TextEdit has a richer door: .show(ui) returns everything it learned while drawing. Three edits.

First — swap ui.add for .show and keep the result:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, the text box

            ui.add(
                egui::TextEdit::multiline(&mut self.text)
                    .font(egui::TextStyle::Monospace)
                    .desired_width(f32::INFINITY),
            );
            let output = egui::TextEdit::multiline(&mut self.text)
                .font(egui::TextStyle::Monospace)
                .desired_width(f32::INFINITY)
                .show(ui);
Two things moved, not one The widget is no longer wrapped in ui.add(…), so the surrounding parentheses and the trailing ); are gone, and the whole chain shifts four spaces to the left — also called a dedent, or an outdent in some editors. It's the same builder chain with .show(ui) on the end instead of being passed to add. Run cargo fmt if the indentation drifts.

Second — report what came back, just above the labels you already have:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, under the text box

            let position = match output.cursor_range {
                Some(range) => format!("offset {}", range.primary.index.0),
                None => "no cursor".to_owned(),
            };
            ui.label(format!("{} bytes", self.text.len()));

Third — fold the position into the byte-count label. Note this replaces the byte-count label; the ui.label(&self.status) line below it is untouched.

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, replacing the byte-count label

            ui.label(&self.status);
            ui.label(format!("{position}  ·  {} bytes", self.text.len()));

The other enum

cursor_range is an Option<CCursorRange>, and Option is Result's sibling. Same idea — an enum with two variants, the compiler forcing you through both — but for absence rather than failure:

TypeVariantsAnswers
Result<T, E>Ok(T) / Err(E)Did it work?
Option<T>Some(T) / NoneIs there one?

There genuinely might not be a cursor — click outside the text box and it loses focus, and there is nothing to report. Languages with null pointers express that by handing you a value that looks fine until you touch it. Rust makes you name the empty case before it will let you at the full one.

range.primary.index.0 — primary is the moving end of a selection (secondary is the anchor), and the .0 unwraps a one-field wrapper type. Stage 2 explains why that wrapper exists; it turns out to be the most important thing on this page.

cargo run
→ click in the text: offset 34 · 61 bytes
→ click outside it: no cursor · 61 bytes

Turn one number into two

A real Ln / Col readout that tracks your cursor.

An offset is where the cursor is; a line and column is where it feels like it is. Converting means walking the text and counting newlines. Two edits.

First — a method, after save in your impl Editor block:

editor/src/main.rsin impl Editor, after save

    }

    /// Turn a character offset into a 1-based line and column.
    fn line_col(&self, char_index: usize) -> (usize, usize) {
        let mut line = 1;
        let mut column = 1;
        for ch in self.text.chars().take(char_index) {
            if ch == '\n' {
                line += 1;
                column = 1;
            } else {
                column += 1;
            }
        }
        (line, column)
    }
}

The return type (usize, usize) is a tuple — two values travelling together without inventing a struct for them. usize is the unsigned integer type used for sizes and indices; it's as wide as a pointer on your machine.

self.text.chars() is an iterator over characters, and .take(char_index) stops it after that many. So the loop walks exactly the text before the cursor, counting newlines. Lines and columns start at 1 because that's what every editor and compiler shows — including the src/main.rs:39:17 in the errors you've been reading.

Second — use it:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, the position match

            let position = match output.cursor_range {
                Some(range) => format!("offset {}", range.primary.index.0),
                Some(range) => {
                    let (line, column) = self.line_col(range.primary.index.0);
                    format!("Ln {line}, Col {column}")
                }
                None => "no cursor".to_owned(),
            };

let (line, column) = … is destructuring: the tuple comes back and is immediately taken apart into two named values. Same pattern-matching machinery as Some(range) on the line above, used for a happier purpose.

cargo run
→ move the cursor around: Ln 2, Col 5 · 61 bytes

You just built the thing in the corner of every editor It is genuinely this: read an offset, walk the text, count newlines. What separates a toy from a real editor isn't the idea — it's that a real one does this correctly for text that isn't English, and does it fast enough on a file with a million lines. Stage 3 is the first of those. The second is lesson 7.

The bug you can't see in English

Understand why char_index is not self.text[..i].

No code change in this stage — this one is about a mistake you haven't made yet, so that you don't. Put a non-English character in your scratch file:

printf 'let x = 1;\nlet café = 2;\nlet y = 3;\n' > editor/scratch.md
→ run, and click just after the é

Look at the two numbers you're now showing. That text is:

bytes = 37, chars = 36

Thirty-seven bytes, thirty-six characters. The é takes two bytes. Rust strings are UTF-8, where a character is one to four bytes depending on what it is — ASCII is one, accented Latin is two, most CJK is three, emoji are four.

So there are two numbers you could call "the position", and they disagree the moment text stops being English:

Index kindCountsWho uses it
Byte offsetBytes of UTF-8text.len(), slicing &text[a..b], files on disk
Char offsetchar valuestext.chars(), egui's cursor
Before reading on: egui hands you char offset 20. What happens if you treat it as a byte offset and write &self.text[..20]?

On that sample you get 19 characters instead of 20 — silently wrong, because the é ate an extra byte. And if the offset had landed inside a multi-byte character rather than after it, the program would have crashed outright.

The silent version is bad. The loud version looks like this — and it's a panic, at runtime, on your user's machine:

thread 'main' panicked at src/main.rs:9:18:
end byte index 8 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 7..9 of string)

This is why line_col takes self.text.chars() and never slices. It counts the same units egui counts, so the two can't drift apart.

Why the API made you write .0

Remember range.primary.index.0, and that odd .0. Here's how egui declares that field:

/// Character offset (NOT byte offset!).
pub index: CharIndex,

// …where CharIndex is:
pub struct CharIndex(pub usize);

It's a usize in a wrapper that exists purely to have a different name. That's a newtype, and the point is that a CharIndex won't compile where a byte index is expected, even though both are just numbers underneath. The capital-letters comment tells you the library authors have been bitten; the type makes sure you can't be, at least not by accident.

There's a third number this lesson is quietly ignoring: what the user sees as a column. A tab may render as eight spaces, and a family emoji is several char values that draw as one glyph. "Column" in a real editor means grapheme clusters, not chars. We'll take that on when we paint text ourselves.

Where you ended up

89 lines, after cargo fmt.

editor/src/main.rs

use eframe::egui;
use std::fs;
use std::io;

struct Editor {
    path: String,
    text: String,
    status: String,
}

impl Editor {
    /// Open a file into a new editor. A failure becomes the buffer contents,
    /// so the window always opens.
    fn open(path: &str) -> Self {
        let text = match fs::read_to_string(path) {
            Ok(contents) => contents,
            Err(error) => format!("could not open {path}\n\n{error}"),
        };
        Self {
            path: path.to_owned(),
            text,
            status: String::new(),
        }
    }

    /// Write the buffer back to the file it came from.
    fn save(&mut self) -> io::Result<()> {
        fs::write(&self.path, &self.text)?;
        self.status = format!("saved {} bytes to {}", self.text.len(), self.path);
        Ok(())
    }

    /// Turn a character offset into a 1-based line and column.
    fn line_col(&self, char_index: usize) -> (usize, usize) {
        let mut line = 1;
        let mut column = 1;
        for ch in self.text.chars().take(char_index) {
            if ch == '\n' {
                line += 1;
                column = 1;
            } else {
                column += 1;
            }
        }
        (line, column)
    }
}

impl eframe::App for Editor {
    fn ui(&mut self, ui: &mut egui::Ui, _frame: &mut eframe::Frame) {
        egui::CentralPanel::default().show(ui, |ui| {
            let save_requested = ui.input(|i| i.modifiers.command && i.key_pressed(egui::Key::S));
            if save_requested && let Err(error) = self.save() {
                self.status = format!("save failed: {error}");
            }

            ui.heading(&self.path);

            let output = egui::TextEdit::multiline(&mut self.text)
                .font(egui::TextStyle::Monospace)
                .desired_width(f32::INFINITY)
                .show(ui);

            let position = match output.cursor_range {
                Some(range) => {
                    let (line, column) = self.line_col(range.primary.index.0);
                    format!("Ln {line}, Col {column}")
                }
                None => "no cursor".to_owned(),
            };

            ui.label(format!("{position}  ·  {} bytes", self.text.len()));
        });
    }
}

fn main() -> eframe::Result {
    let options = eframe::NativeOptions {
        viewport: egui::ViewportBuilder::default().with_inner_size([800.0, 600.0]),
        ..Default::default()
    };

    eframe::run_native(
        "editor",
        options,
        Box::new(|_cc| Ok(Box::new(Editor::open("scratch.md")))),
    )
}

Check yourself

Why is cursor_range an Option rather than a plain value?

  • The text box may not have focus at all
  • Cursors are expensive to compute each frame
  • Selections can span more than a single line
  • Immediate mode discards widget state yearly

Click outside the text box and there is genuinely no cursor to report. Option makes that case a thing you must name before the compiler lets you at the value — the same trick Result plays with failure. ↑ Review: Option vs Result (stage 1)

Your text is "let café = 2;". How do len() and chars().count() compare?

  • len() is larger — é takes two bytes
  • They agree; both count characters in order
  • len() is smaller because it skips accents
  • They agree unless the string contains any emoji

len() returns bytes. Rust strings are UTF-8, so a character is one to four bytes; é is two. That's why the sample measures 37 bytes but 36 chars, and why mixing the two indices silently misplaces the cursor. ↑ Review: byte vs char offsets (stage 3)

From lesson 3: what does ? do to an Err inside save?

  • Returns it immediately to the caller
  • Prints it and continues to the next line
  • Converts it into a default success value
  • Stores it on the struct for later reading

Early return. save can't know whether a failed write deserves a message or a retry, so it propagates upward to the code that does — which is also why the success status never gets set on a failed save. ↑ Review: what ? expands to (lesson 3, stage 4)

Read this before lesson 5

Primary source: The Rust Programming Language, 8.2 — Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings.

Short, and squarely the thing you just met. It works through why Rust refuses to let you index a string with s[0] at all, and lays out the three ways to look at text — bytes, chars, and grapheme clusters. The section on grapheme clusters is the column-counting problem this lesson deferred.

I'm your teacher here — ask me things. Stage 3 has no code in it, which is unusual — if a stage that only explains a bug felt like filler, tell me and I'll make the case for it. And if output.cursor_range is None when you expect a cursor, that's worth a message; focus behaviour is fiddly.
